newsitem.title: CHINA: Contacts resume over Korea defector in China.
newsitem.headline: Contacts resume over Korea defector in China.

text.p: Contacts between Beijing and Seoul over the fate of the most senior official to flee North Korea resumed on Wednesday after being stalled by the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, South Korean officials said.

Pyongyang's top ideological theoretician Hwang Jang-yop has been stranded in Seoul's mission in Beijing since he plunged ties between China and the two rival Koreas into crisis by seeking asylum there on February 12.
Deng's death last week put negotiations over Hwang's fate largely on hold, officials said, but six days of mourning for the Chinese patriarch ended with his funeral on Tuesday.
"Contacts between Seoul and Beijing have resumed, but so far no important developments have been reported," South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said in Seoul.
Officials of Seoul's Beijing embassy were unable to comment on whether formal negotiations over Hwang's fate had restarted, but said Deng's cremation and funeral had slowed contacts.
"For the last two days, you can guess, the high-level talks were not progressed," said Chang Moon-ik, spokesman of the South Korean embassy in Beijing.
"We want to finish this event as soon as possible, but we don't know when," he said.

Chinese police backed by armoured personnel carriers and a riot truck maintained their tight guard around the South Korean mission on a cold, grey Wednesday, sealing off surrounding streets in the normally placid tree-lined embassy district.
Vanloads of police also kept a close watch on Pyongyang's embassy just a few kilometres away.
Hwang's defection has entangled China in the decades-old enmity between Seoul and Pyongyang, forcing Beijing to choose between an old communist ally and a new capitalist friend.
Analysts say China will in the end almost certainly allow Hwang, the architect of North Korea's governing ideology of strict self-reliance, to go to Seoul.
But Beijing also wants to help its Stalinist neighbour save face by being seen to give Pyongyang's concerns due attention.

"It may take some time before the issue is resolved as the Chinese Government is taking pains to settle it in a manner that doesn't get on North Korea's nerves," the South Korean Yonhap agency quoted an official at Seoul's Beijing mission as saying.

Hwang's defection threw extra strain on ties between the two Koreas, which are still technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended only in a truce, but there have been signs in recent days that the crisis may be easing.
Pyongyang, which at first insisted that Hwang had been kidnapped by South Korean agents, softened its stance last week by vowing to dismiss the scholarly ideologue if he had in fact defected.
Korea analysts said on Wednesday that Pyongyang had allowed a government delegation to travel abroad for the first time since clamping down on foreign travel after Hwang's defection.
Tokyo-based Radiopress analysts said a Foreign Ministry delegation headed by Vice Minister Kim Chang-ryong left Pyongyang by train bound for Switzerland, Germany and Norway.

Seoul has moved to reduce tensions with gestures towards Pyongyang, allowing businessmen to become the first South Koreans to visit the North since an incursion by a North Korean submarine froze contacts last September.
But South Korean police have also stepped up a manhunt for two suspected assassins from the North after the death of a Pyongyang defector shot earlier this month.
Police were working on the theory that Pyongyang ordered its agents to murder Lee Han-yong as a warning to South Korea and other North Korean escapees after Hwang's defection.
